title: Luther and Melanchthon again leave no empty reprobation against eternal ordination
pass_a_gloss: With Luther again, and those who vote with him, the dispute is not about an empty reprobation, but about God's eternal ordination and arrangement of all things, even as to the damnation of the reprobate, the hardening of Pharaoh, the betrayal by Judas, and so on. Places from Luther and Melanchthon may be seen either in the Apology of the Rinteln men, or in Calixtus, Consultation on Tolerating the Reformed, pages about 12, 13, 14 — to say nothing of our own writers. For example Melanchthon: Judas's betrayal is no less God's work than Paul's conversion; all things happen according to divine predestination, according to which the Lord has worked all things for Himself, even the wicked for the day of evil, and so on. But Luther: God by His will necessarily makes us damnable, so that He seems to delight in the torments of the wretched; God does not will the death of the sinner by the Word, yet He does will it by an unsearchable will; whatever is said to excuse God is said in vain, and so on, lest He Himself be the author and the blame of our hardening; if God foresaw that Judas would be a traitor, Judas necessarily became a traitor, and so on. And more excerpts of this kind are taken even from the single book On the Bondage of the Will, volume II, first Wittenberg edition.
pass_b_english: Again with Luther and those who vote with him, the fight is not over a vacant reprobation, but over God's eternal ordination — His disposal of everything, even the damnation of the reprobate, Pharaoh's hardening, Judas's betrayal, and the rest.
See the passages from Luther and Melanchthon in the Rinteln Apology, or in Calixtus's Consultation on Tolerating the Reformed, around pages 12–14 — not to mention our own writers.

Melanchthon, for example: Judas's betrayal is no less God's work than Paul's conversion; everything falls out by divine predestination, by which the Lord has worked all things for Himself, even the wicked for the day of evil.

Luther, for his part: by His will God necessarily makes us damnable, so that He seems to take pleasure in the torments of the miserable; God does not will the sinner's death by the Word, yet He does will it by an unsearchable will; whatever is said to clear God is said in vain — lest He Himself be made the author and the blame of our hardening; if God foresaw that Judas would betray, Judas necessarily became a traitor.
Still more of this is drawn from the single book On the Bondage of the Will, volume II, first Wittenberg edition.
source_text: Cum Luthero rursum, & ὁμοψήφοις, lis de Reprobatione nulla, seu aeternâ Dei ordinatione, dispositione omnium, etiam quoad damnationem reproborum, indurationem Pharaonis, proditionem Judae, &c. Loca ex Luthero, & Melanchthone, vide vel in Apologia Rintelensium, aut apud Calixtum, Consultat. de Tolerantia Reform. p. m. 12. 13. 14. ut nostros taceam. V. gr. Melanchthon; Non minùs Judae proditionem, quàm Pauli conversionem Dei opus esse; Evenire omnia juxta divinam Praedestinationem, secundum quam Universa propter seipsum operatus est Dominus, etiam impium ad diem mali, &c. Lutherus verò; Deus suâ voluntate nos necessariò damnabiles facit; ut videatur delectari cruciatibus miserorum: Deus non vult mortem peccatoris Verbô, vult autem Voluntate imperescrutabili: Frustrà dicitur, quicquid dicitur, pro excusando Deo, &c. ne ipse sit auctor & culpa nostrae Indurationis: Si praescivit Deus Judam fore proditorem, necessariò Judas fiebat proditor, &c. Et quae plura excerpta sunt, vel ex uno Libro de Servo Arbitrio, Tomo II. Ed. I. Wittenb.
